summary: Sayings on God’s hold over every heart, justice ranked above sacrifice, and the fate of one deaf to the poor.

context.title: Sayings on the heart and the neighbour
paragraphs: Chapters 10:1 to 22:16 form a collection of separate sayings under a fresh heading, the proverbs of Solomon. [c1] Each saying is complete in itself, though the collector sometimes sets sayings on one subject side by side. [c2] Almost all are two-line couplets, the second line either contrasting with the first or carrying it further. [c3]

First comes God’s hand on the heart: the king’s heart in verse 1, every heart weighed in verse 2, a near repeat of 16:2. [c4] Verse 3 ranks doing justice above sacrifice, as Samuel, Hosea and Micah do. [c5] This is a ranking, not a rejection of worship: Barnes notes it comes from the king who built the temple. [c6]

Verses 10-13 turn to the neighbour: the wicked person craves evil and shows a neighbour no favour. [c7] The last saying warns that whoever ignores the cry of the poor will cry out and go unheard. [c8] The poor man, the dal, is one without support or means of living. [c9] Keil and Delitzsch draw the moral: only the merciful find mercy. [c10]

translationNotes.summary: Peleg is an irrigation channel: the picture is water steered by hand, not a river in flood.
translationNotes.body: Peleg is a channel or canal, often a small cut made for irrigation. [c11] The comparison comes from watering a garden, where the gardener opens one little channel and closes another. [c12] Perowne notes that the irrigator alone decides where the water flows. [c13] So the king, who seems to answer to no one, is steered by God as easily as water in a ditch. [c14]

translationNotes.summary: Hebrew calls the LORD a “weigher of hearts”, using a verb for measuring and weighing.
translationNotes.body: Tokhen is a participle of takan, to measure, weigh or estimate. [c15] The same title is used with spirits in 16:2 and with hearts in 24:12, so God is pictured as the one who weighs. [c15][c16] Set against the first line, where a person’s own way looks right to him, the saying warns against self-deception. [c17]

translationNotes.summary: One Hebrew word, two readings: the ploughed field of the wicked, or their lamp of prosperity.
translationNotes.body: With a change of vowels the word can be read as freshly broken ground or as lamp. [c18] The Greek and Latin versions read lamp, and the Cambridge Bible prefers it. [c19] A lamp burning in the house stood for prosperity, so the shining success of the wicked is itself called sin. [c20] Keil and Delitzsch keep the field: all the husbandry of the godless is sin. [c21]

translationNotes.summary: Hevel, the breath or vapour of Ecclesiastes, pictures wealth won by lies drifting away.
translationNotes.body: Hevel is vapour or breath, and figuratively vanity; Ecclesiastes uses it nearly forty times. [c22] Read literally, the line runs “a vapour dispersed; seekers of death”. [c23] By the change of one letter, the Greek and Latin versions read snares of death instead. [c24] Either way, wealth gained by lying is as unstable as breath and ends in death. [c25]

claims.text: Proverbs 10:1 to 22:16 is a collection of separate sayings marked by a new heading, the proverbs of Solomon.
Each verse of the collection is complete in itself, though the collector seems to have grouped sayings on the same subject.
The collection consists of two-line sayings (distichs), mostly antithetic in Proverbs 10-15 and synthetic in Proverbs 16:1-22:16.
Proverbs 21:2 repeats Proverbs 16:2 almost exactly.
Proverbs 21:3 gives doing justice and right pre-eminence over sacrifice, a theme shared with 1 Samuel 15:22, Hosea 6:6 and Micah 6:6-8.
Proverbs 21:3 ranks justice above sacrifice rather than rejecting worship; Barnes notes that it comes from the king who built the temple and offered sacrifices beyond counting (1 Kgs 8:5).
Proverbs 21:10 says the soul of the wicked desires evil and his neighbour finds no favour in his eyes.
Proverbs 21:13 warns that one who stops his ear at the cry of the poor will himself cry and not be answered, a retribution on the unmerciful.
The דַּל of Proverbs 21:13 is one without support and means of subsistence.
Keil and Delitzsch comment on Proverbs 21:13 that only the merciful find mercy, citing Matthew 5:7.
Hebrew פֶּלֶג means a channel or canal, a small channel of water as in irrigation.
The comparison in Proverbs 21:1 is drawn from irrigation, with little channels under the gardener’s control.
The irrigator has complete control over the water supply.
The heart of the king, who might seem to have no superior, is directed by God.
The verb תָּכַן means to regulate, measure or estimate; its participle is used of the LORD weighing spirits in Proverbs 16:2 and hearts in Proverbs 21:2 and 24:12.
In Proverbs 21:2 God is called a weigher of hearts.
Proverbs 21:2 sets a person’s own view of his way against God’s weighing and warns against self-deception.
With a change in its vowel points, the Hebrew word in Proverbs 21:4 can mean either the fallow or broken-up field (tillage) or a lamp.
The Septuagint and the Vulgate read lamp in Proverbs 21:4, and the Cambridge Bible prefers that rendering.
A lamp burning in the house is a symbol of the prosperity of an individual.
Keil and Delitzsch read the word as the field, so that the whole husbandry of the godless is sin.
Hebrew הֶבֶל means vapour or breath, figuratively vanity, and Ecclesiastes uses it nearly forty times.
Proverbs 21:6b reads literally “a vapour dispersed; seekers of death”.
By the change of a letter in the Hebrew, the Septuagint and Vulgate read snares of death in Proverbs 21:6.
Wealth obtained by a lying tongue is as evanescent and unstable as breath and ends in death.
